title: Fort Corchaug
summary: Fort Corchaug is a protected archaeological site associated with a small seventeenth-century Corchaug refuge and working place. Earthworks, palisade trenches, shell-working debris, beads, and Native and European objects connect the place to defense, wampum production, and exchange during a period of warfare, epidemics, and colonial land pressure.
activity_update_summary: Added a dedicated, cited introduction explaining Fort Corchaug's longer Native landscape, archaeological evidence, likely use as a temporary refuge and working place, colonial-era pressures, and the later Southold records.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Shell debris, abrading stones, and finished beads show that this refuge was also a working place, while imported goods and defensive earthworks document a period of exchange and danger. Because colonial records preserve only fragments of Corchaug life, the site's intact archaeology provides evidence that surviving paperwork leaves out. Fort Corchaug is one place within a continuing community history, not proof of disappearance or control over regional trade.
introduction_title: A refuge, working place, and longer landscape
introduction_content: Fort Corchaug preserves a small fortified place used by Corchaug people during the first half of the seventeenth century, within a landscape whose archaeology records at least 6,000 years of Native use. Excavators documented an earthen enclosure, palisade trenches, pits, hearths, a midden, and shell-working debris. Sparse remains inside and possible house patterns outside led the National Historic Landmark study to interpret it mainly as a temporary refuge and working place rather than a permanent village. Whelk columellae, abrading stones, and finished beads document wampum production; Native and European objects show wider exchange. The study connects this period with regional warfare, epidemics, and Dutch and English colonial pressure. Town records it cites describe most Corchaug people relocating to Hog Neck in 1664 and to Indian Neck by 1685; 40 Native people remained recorded in Southold in 1698, and land claims continued into 1764. This protected site is one place within a broader Corchaug community history.
